full_text:
Inter-Cluster Coordination Group - Bangladesh 
This report was produced by the Inter-Cluster Coordination Group in collaboration with cluster coordinators and humanitarian partners, members of the Humanitarian Coordination Task Team. Highlights • An estimated 1.11 million people have been affected across 10 districts, including more than 12,900 persons with disabilities. As of 12 July, 51 deaths had been reported in connection with the floods and landslides. • At least 38,422 people are staying in 1,047 formal evacuation shelters. • Flooded roads, damaged bridges, landslides and waterlogging continue to constrain humanitarian access. BMD forecasts continued rainfall until 17 July, including episodes of heavy to very heavy rainfall in Sylhet and Chattogram divisions, which may further aggravate flooding and landslide conditions in districts already affected. • Preliminary Government reports indicate that 29,741 houses were damaged in Bandarban and Chattogram. • The Government has deployed 516 medical teams across 50 affected upazilas, while humanitarian partners are scaling up assistance with food, cash, shelter, protection, and water, sanitation, and hygiene. 
1.11M *Affected People 38.4K Internally Displaced 1K Active Evacuation Shelters 3.5K Damaged Waterpoints 12.4K Damaged Latrines 
Bangladesh: Flash Flood and Landslides Situation Report #1 13 July 2026 
*Affected population estimates are based on spatial analysis of flood inundation relative to the total mouza area within affected upazilas, overlaid with Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief situation report data and validated by local administrations. Flood extent was derived from Sentinel-1 satellite imagery dated 10 July 2026, accessed through the GFM service of GLOFAS.
Inter-Cluster Coordination Group Situation Report | 1 
 Inter-Cluster Coordination Group - Bangladesh 
Situation Overview Under the influence of an active southwest monsoon and a steep pressure gradient over the North Bay of Bengal and adjoining areas, heavy to very heavy rainfall has persisted across Chattogram Division and other parts of Bangladesh since 5 July 2026. Prolonged rainfall, upstream runoff, and flows from hilly catchments have triggered flash floods, waterlogging, rising river levels, and landslides, particularly in Bandarban, Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Khagrachhari, and Rangamati. The floods and landslides have damaged infrastructure, disrupted road and rail connectivity and constrained access to affected communities. The Bangladesh Meteorological Department (BMD), forecasts continued rainfall until 17 July 2026, including episodes of heavy to very heavy rainfall in Sylhet and Chattogram divisions, which may further aggravate flooding and landslide conditions in already affected districts. Water, sanitation and hygiene services have been disrupted across 27 upazilas in 10 districts. In several areas, infrastructure remains submerged, while water sources have been damaged or contaminated by floodwater carrying faecal matter, agricultural chemicals, industrial waste and other pollutants. As of 12 July, the Department of Public Health Engineering (DPHE) reported that more than 12,360 latrines and 3,583 waterpoints had been fully or partially damaged. Preliminary Government reports indicate that 15,881 houses were damaged in Bandarban and 13,860 in Chattogram. The full extent and severity of housing damage remain unclear, as standing water and access constraints continue to delay detailed assessments. Inter-Cluster Coordination Group Situation Report | 1 
 Inter-Cluster Coordination Group - Bangladesh 
Following the heavy rainfall forecast issued on 5 July, the Ministry of Disaster Management and Relief (MoDMR), the Department of Disaster Management (DDM), the BMD and the Flood Forecasting and Warning Centre (FFWC) convened a series of coordination meetings. The Ministry activated the National Disaster Response Coordination Centre on a 24-hour basis and circulated emergency contact numbers. District administrations also convened disaster management committees to coordinate early warning dissemination, evacuation, shelter management, hot meals, and rescue operations, with support from the Bangladesh Army, the Bangladesh Red Crescent Society (BDRCS), Border Guard Bangladesh, the Fire Service and Civil Defence, police, and upazila administrations. On 12 July, the Prime Minister’s Office convened a virtual meeting to review the impact of the floods, including waterlogging, infrastructure damage, shelter conditions, rescue operations, relief distribution and medical services. Authorities were instructed to prioritise the protection of lives and property, accelerate the delivery of food, safe water, medicines and healthcare, and ensure that shelters provide adequate safety, sanitation, electricity, communication and support for vulnerable groups. Agencies were also directed to strengthen coordination, maintain operational readiness, monitor forecasts and river levels, and ensure transparent relief delivery. Between 7 and 12 July, the Government of Bangladesh allocated a cumulative BDT 17.5 million (approximately US$142,276) and 3,250 metric tons of rice to support response efforts in seven flood- and rainfall-affected districts. Chattogram received the largest allocation, totalling BDT 6.5 million and 1,200 metric tons of rice, followed by Cox’s Bazar with BDT 3 million and 450 metric tons. Bandarban and Khagrachhari each received BDT 2 million and 400 metric tons of rice, while Rangamati received BDT 2.5 million and 500 metric tons. Further allocations included BDT 1 million and 200 metric tons of rice for Moulvibazar, and BDT 500,000 and 100 metric tons for Habiganj. The assistance was released through successive general and rain- and flood-response allocations on 7, 9, 10 and 12 July, allowing additional resources to be directed to districts as the situation evolved. Humanitarian Response On 11 July, the Inter-Cluster Coordination Group (ICCG) convened an ad hoc meeting to review the evolving situation, anticipatory action activations and initial updates from clusters and partners. The meeting agreed to strengthen monitoring, consolidate information on response activities, priority needs and gaps, and prepare the first ICCG Situation Report. The displacement management, health, logistics, shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene clusters subsequently convened emergency coordination meetings to review field information, identify operational constraints and coordinate follow-up actions. The Needs Assessment and Information Management Working Group (NA/IMWG) issued two Flash Updates on 9 and 12 July and continues to consolidate available data, while a multi-sectoral assessment will be considered once access conditions permit. The Anticipatory Action Technical Working Group (AATWG) remains in close coordination with agencies implementing active anticipatory action frameworks, sharing trigger updates and monitoring developments. The ICCG Secretariat continues to coordinate with cluster coordinators, the BMD, the DDM, the MoDMR, the NGO Affairs Bureau, and Deputy Commissioners across all ten affected districts to support a coherent response. Start Fund Bangladesh has allocated £800,000 (approximately US$1.07 million) to support response activities in Bandarban, Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar and Rangamati. The funding will primarily support cash assistance, food, non-food items and early warning dissemination.
Inter-Cluster Coordination Group Situation Report | 1 
 Inter-Cluster Coordination Group - Bangladesh 
This report presents the national response to floods and landslides across affected districts. Data from the Rohingya refugee camps are reported separately and are not included here. Anticipatory Action Flash floods in the south-east and Chattogram Hill Tracts: WFP activated anticipatory action (AA) and shock-responsive social protection (SRSP) in Bandarban on 10 July, ahead of peak flooding, reaching 15,000 households through AA and 859 through SRSP with multipurpose cash grants of BDT 5,000 per household and early warning messages. Activities covered Bandarban Sadar and Lama upazilas. Flash floods in the north-eastern Haor region: As of 11 July 2026, the pre-activation trigger had been reached in Sunamganj Sadar and Tahirpur upazilas. Readiness triggers had been reached in Mohanganj (Netrokona), Nalitabari (Sherpur), Derai and Sunamganj Sadar (Sunamganj), and Gowainghat, Kanaighat and Sylhet Sadar (Sylhet). BDRCS disseminated warnings in Sunamganj and Sylhet; CARE Bangladesh mobilised volunteers, assessed shelters and pre-positioned four boats in Derai and Gowainghat, targeting 18,500 people; UN Women reached approximately 300 households in Kanaighat; and World Vision reached around 50,000 people with warnings, pre-positioned 1,000 hygiene kits, validated lists for 700 households, and prepared to evacuate up to 2,000 households. The activation trigger has not yet been reached. The Anticipatory Action Technical Working Group continues monitoring with the Regional Integrated Multi-Hazard Early Warning System and the FFWC; cash assistance and evacuation support will follow if the trigger is reached. Landslides: Caritas and Save the Children activated landslide anticipatory action under the draft National Landslide Early Action Protocol. Save the Children provided BDT 6,000 per household1 to 400 at-risk households, in line with the 2026 Inter-Cluster Coordination Group-endorsed transfer value, alongside early warning and evacuation support in Bandarban, Chattogram and Rangamati. BDRCS supported warning and evacuation activities in Chattogram and Cox’s Bazar. Caritas provided early warning, shelter inspections and evacuation support in Bandarban and Cox’s Bazar. Gaps and constraints: The Flash Flood National Early Action Protocol remains unendorsed and is limited to the north-eastern Haor region, constraining government-led implementation. The limited presence of AA actors/organisations also reduced early warning coverage in triggered areas, while no corresponding protocol exists for the Chattogram Hill Tracts. 
 1Save the Children has already adhered to the 2026 anticipatory action cash transfer value endorsed this year by the Inter-Cluster Coordination Group.
Inter-Cluster Coordination Group Situation Report | 1 
 Inter-Cluster Coordination Group - Bangladesh 
 Child Protection in Emergency Cluster Needs: • Prevent family separation and provide tracing, reunification, case management and referrals to food, health and cash assistance. • Ensure safe, accessible and dignified shelter conditions for children and adolescents, including protection from sexual harassment, exploitation, abuse and neglect and access to confidential reporting mechanisms. • Provide family and dignity kits, psychosocial first aid and support, and accessible services for children with disabilities. Response: • The Department of Social Services, Ministry of Women and Children Affairs and UNICEF maintained child protection services in Chattogram and Hathazari through 17 social workers and 176 volunteers. In the Chattogram Hill Tracts, three Child Rights Officers, nine Community Hub Organisers and 200 caregivers continued outreach, while psychosocial, recreational, family and dignity kits were pre-positioned. • Plan International mobilised more than 150 staff and volunteers across the upazilas of Chakaria, Matamuhuri, and Teknaf. Activities reached 2,662 people with disaster risk reduction messages, 1,465 with psychosocial first aid, and 1,955 with psychosocial support; 14 children were referred, and 10 received emergency kits. • ActionAid is assessing needs in Pekua Upazila and verifying the situation of 1,025 sponsored children. Assistance for approximately 500 families is planned, while 150 dignity kits and cash grants for 450 households were provided in Teknaf. • The Centre for Services and Information on Disability estimates that 523 children with disabilities are affected across 12 districts and continues supporting affected families with essential services and accessible evacuation. Gaps & Constraints: • Overcrowded shelters, inadequate lighting and damaged or inaccessible water, sanitation and hygiene facilities are increasing risks of violence, exploitation, family separation and loss of privacy, particularly for women, girls and children with disabilities. • Safe spaces, confidential reporting, survivor care and mental health and psychosocial support services require restoration. • Disrupted services and livelihood losses are increasing risks of child marriage, child labour, unsafe migration and exploitation. Displacement Management Cluster Needs: • At least 1,047 formal shelters are hosting 38,422 displaced people: 6,250 in Bandarban, 21,900 in Chattogram, 1,580 in Cox’s Bazar, 2,883 in Khagrachhari, 2,172 in Moulvibazar and 3,637 in Rangamati. Essential services and supplies are required across these sites. Response: • BDRCS mobilised more than 3,500 volunteers across 12 units for search, rescue and evacuation, assisting 200 people in Bandarban and 300 in Rangamati. BDRCS plans to reach 10 per cent of the affected population, prioritising displaced people.
Inter-Cluster Coordination Group Situation Report | 1 
 Inter-Cluster Coordination Group - Bangladesh 
• IOM is clearing 10 drains linked to 5 cyclone shelters in Cox’s Bazar District to reduce waterlogging and maintain safe access, while supporting the dissemination of early warnings with shelter management committees, local volunteers, and disaster management committees. • The Norwegian Refugee Council distributed dry food to displaced people in evacuation shelters across Bandarban. • Uttaran is supporting community preparedness through early warning dissemination, risk awareness and outreach, encouraging families in high-risk areas to move to safer locations. • Plan International Bangladesh provided dry food and essential non-food items to displaced families in Cox’s Bazar, including candles, lighters, safe drinking water, water purification tablets and sanitary pads. • Save the Children reached more than 705,600 people with voice messages and early warning information. Approximately 415 community volunteers were mobilised to support localised early warning dissemination, household preparedness, evacuation of over 1,300 households, and community-level risk communication. Ashika, RIMES and Young Power in Social Action (YPSA) supported the implementation of these activities. Gaps & Constraints: • At least 150,000 people reportedly remain stranded across the affected areas and require urgent evacuation support, including additional boats. • Additional assistance is needed for people staying with relatives, neighbours and host communities, indicating that displacement exceeds the formal shelter caseload. Education Cluster Needs: • An estimated 228,698 learners may be affected. At least 1,276 schools are temporarily closed, disrupting learning for approximately 176,400 students, mainly at pre-primary and primary levels. • Schools used as temporary shelters require timely handover, cleaning, minor repairs and safety checks before classes resume. Response: • Education authorities and partners are disseminating life-saving messages on floods, cyclones, landslides and snakebites. • Education in Emergencies kits and home-based learning packages are being prepared, with parents and caregivers encouraged to support learning during closures. • The Cluster is coordinating with government counterparts and district and upazila education offices to safeguard learning materials, support referrals and facilitate safe reopening. Gaps & Constraints: • Limited real-time data and access constraints are hampering assessments, response planning and monitoring. • The absence of a nationally agreed alternative-learning approach and dedicated response funding limits learning continuity and scale-up. • Continued use of schools as shelters may delay reopening and increase cleaning and repair needs. Food Security Cluster Needs:
Inter-Cluster Coordination Group Situation Report | 1 
 Inter-Cluster Coordination Group - Bangladesh 
• Priority assistance is required across 59 upazilas in Bandarban, Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Habiganj, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar and Rangamati. • Ready-to-eat food, cooking kits and clean fuel are urgently needed for displaced households and families unable to cook or access markets. • Waterproof storage for seeds and fertilisers, livestock feed, temporary animal shelters and veterinary support are needed to protect agricultural livelihoods. Response: • ActionAid Bangladesh is preparing multipurpose cash grants for 500 households in Magnama and Rajakhali unions of Pekua Upazila, Cox’s Bazar. • BDRCS allocated BDT 2 million for dry and processed food in Bandarban, Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Habiganj, Khagrachhari, Moulvibazar and Rangamati. • BRAC distributed dry food to 3,100 families across five districts and allocated an additional BDT 3.3 million for assistance in Bandarban, Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar and Rangamati. • COAST Foundation provided cash to seven families in Rohingya Camps 3 and 5 and plans to distribute dry food and drinking water in Kutubdia Upazila. • WFP plans to distribute high-energy biscuits to approximately 24,200 households in Bandarban, Chattogram and Rangamati. • World Vision Bangladesh distributed 770 dry food packages and provided food to 300 people in Bandarban and assisted 500 households in Cox’s Bazar. Gaps & Constraints: • Heavy rainfall, damaged roads, disrupted river crossings and unsafe terrain are delaying assessments and assistance. • Limited sectoral data and humanitarian presence, particularly in the Chattogram Hill Tracts, constrain prioritisation and coverage. • Available resources and pre-positioned dry and ready-to-eat food stocks remain insufficient. • Flooding, market closures and supply-chain disruptions have reduced the feasibility of cash-based assistance in some areas. Gender-based Violence Cluster Needs: • Dignity items and psychosocial support are urgently required for women, girls and other at-risk groups who have lost homes or belongings. • Evacuation shelters need safe spaces, adequate lighting, trained women and men volunteers, accessible sex-segregated facilities and functioning gender-based violence referral pathways. • Bandhu Welfare Society and CBO Network (Community-Based Organisation) estimates that 200 gender-diverse people require assistance across Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Kishoreganj, Netrokona and Rangamati. Response: • Bandhu Social Welfare Society and Community-Based Organisation Bangladesh are assessing and documenting the needs of gender-diverse people in Bandarban, Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Khagrachhari, Kishoreganj, Netrokona and Rangamati. • BDRCS distributed approximately 2,000 sanitary pads across 12 affected districts. • Concern Worldwide is supporting 6,000 households in Noakhali Sadar and Sonaimuri with food, household items, sanitary pads, safe water and referrals.
Inter-Cluster Coordination Group Situation Report | 1 
 Inter-Cluster Coordination Group - Bangladesh 
• GRAUS and Manusher Jonno Foundation are supporting evacuations and gender-based violence response and referrals in Bandarban and Rangamati. • Oxfam is preparing a Rapid Gender Analysis alongside a Rapid Needs Assessment in Satkania Upazila, Chattogram. • UNFPA is distributing 800 dignity kits in Khagrachhari and plans to distribute 1,000 additional kits in Bandarban and Noakhali, 1,950 menstrual hygiene management kits, and cash assistance to 220 recipients and 30 girls with disabilities. Gaps & Constraints: • Difficult terrain, inaccessible shelters, language barriers and limited mobile access are restricting evacuation and early warning, particularly for Indigenous women and girls, older persons and persons with disabilities. • Crowded shelters often lack safe toilets, menstrual hygiene materials, private breastfeeding spaces, and controls on outsider access, increasing protection risks. • Damaged roads, limited transport, and disrupted crisis centres, police help desks, and referral services are restricting life-saving care for pregnant women and survivors. • Gender-diverse people, including Hijra communities, face exclusion from rescue operations and shelters due to stigma and discrimination. Health Cluster Needs: • Replenish medicines and supplies and assess damaged or inundated health facilities to sustain services and guide rehabilitation. • Strengthen surveillance for diarrhoea, dengue, measles and other waterborne and vector-borne diseases. • Provide catch-up vaccination through the Expanded Programme on Immunisation for children who missed routine sessions. Response: • The Government deployed 516 medical teams across 50 upazilas in five districts of Chattogram Division, providing services in shelters and affected communities. • Government health authorities activated control rooms at affected Upazila Health Complexes, established district-level coordination groups and continued health education and risk communication. • Local health authorities are coordinating with the Ansar and Village Defence Party, BDRCS, non-governmental organisations, the Scouts, and other stakeholders. • WHO divisional coordinators and Surveillance and Immunisation Medical Officers are supporting coordination, information management and response, and also maintaining constant coordination with local health cluster partners. Gaps & Constraints: • Inadequate sanitation and waste management in some shelters may increase the risk of outbreaks. • Incomplete facility assessments and weaknesses in real-time reporting and information management continue to limit the ability to make evidence-based decisions. Logistics Cluster Needs:
Inter-Cluster Coordination Group Situation Report | 1 
 Inter-Cluster Coordination Group - Bangladesh 
• Verified information on roads, bridges and alternative routes is required to support assessments and response planning. Boat support and coordination with the MoDMR, Armed Forces and other authorities may be needed if road access worsens. Response: • The National Logistics Cluster convened an emergency meeting on 12 July, shared logistics assessments for Bandarban, Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Khagrachhari and Rangamati, and continues information-sharing through its established channels. • Islamic Relief Bangladesh is conducting field assessments and has placed suppliers on standby, pending approval to activate in Cox’s Bazar. • Oxfam is planning an assessment in Satkania Upazila, Chattogram. Gaps & Constraints: • Road access remains volatile in Bandarban, Chattogram, Cox’s Bazar, Khagrachhari and Rangamati, requiring continued verification of roads, bridges, and alternative routes. • Logistics requirements remain under assessment; no requests for common services have been received. Nutrition Cluster Needs: • Screen 84,000 children aged 6–59 months and provide infant and young child feeding counselling for 44,000 children aged 0–23 months. • Manage 5,000 cases of severe acute malnutrition over three months and provide small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements to 34,000 children. Response: • The Institute of Public Health Nutrition responded to reports of powdered milk distribution in Bandarban by issuing guidance to Deputy Commissioners’ Offices across the Chattogram Hill Tracts on compliance with the Breast-milk Substitutes Code. Cluster members were asked to monitor compliance. • The Nutrition Cluster shared emergency nutrition messages and distributed 28 cartons of therapeutic milk to Chattogram, Cumilla, Feni and Khagrachhari. • Through its co-lead, the United Nations Children’s Fund, the Cluster pre-positioned 480 tins of F-75, sufficient for approximately 240 cases; 120 tins of F-100; 14 height boards; two weighing scales; three nutrition kits; and 45 packs of mid-upper arm circumference tapes at the Chattogram Medical Sub-Depot. National stocks include 1,500 cartons of small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements, sufficient for around 10,000 children for three months, and 800 cartons of F-75 and 400 of F-100. Gaps & Constraints: • The Cluster has no dedicated emergency funding, and available small-quantity lipid-based nutrient supplements remain insufficient. Shelter Cluster Needs:
Inter-Cluster Coordination Group Situation Report | 1 
 Inter-Cluster Coordination Group - Bangladesh 
• Housing in the affected areas is highly vulnerable, with an estimated 69 per cent of structures classified as jhupri houses2, which are particularly susceptible to flooding and landslides. • As of 13 July 2026, preliminary Government reports indicate that 15,881 houses were damaged in Bandarban and 13,860 in Chattogram. Significant impacts were also reported in Bandarban Sadar and Lama upazilas in Bandarban; Anwara, Banshkhali, Chandanaish, Lohagara and Satkania in Chattogram; Chakaria, Kutubdia, Matamuhuri, Pekua and Ramu in Cox’s Bazar; Dighinala, Khagrachhari Sadar and Mahalchhari in Khagrachhari; and Baghaichhari and Bilaichhari in Rangamati. • Detailed assessments remain ongoing, as standing water continues to restrict access and delay verification of the full extent and severity of housing damage. • Priority needs include tents, tarpaulins, shelter repair toolkits, essential household items, kitchen sets and cash assistance. To address immediate shelter recovery needs, the district administrations have requested 1,200 bundles of corrugated galvanised iron sheets for Bandarban and 4,350 bundles for Chattogram. Response: • Pending verified damage and needs data, partners are reviewing capacities and maintaining readiness to mobilise targeted shelter support in priority locations. Gaps & Constraints: • Detailed assessments are ongoing, but preliminary reports indicate significant damage to housing. • Damaged roads, disrupted communications, and limited verified data are constraining access, planning and targeting. Water, Sanitation and Hygiene Cluster Needs: • Safe drinking water and emergency sanitation, including temporary or mobile latrines and desludging, are urgently required in shelters and remote, waterlogged communities. • Comprehensive hygiene kits, including menstrual hygiene materials, and stronger solid waste and environmental sanitation measures are needed. • Damaged water and sanitation systems require rapid rehabilitation, alongside expanded hygiene promotion and disease prevention in remote hill and landslide-prone areas. Response: • The PDHE, in coordination with district administrations, UNICEF, and Cluster partners, distributed or pre-positioned more than 1.89 million water purification tablets and deployed three mobile water treatment plants in Bandarban, Chattogram, and Cox’s Bazar. • Partners distributed 2,000 jerrycans, 128 hygiene kits and 850 family hygiene kits in Bandarban, Khagrachhari and Rangamati; 2,500 light hygiene kits are planned for affected areas. • A total of 7,200 sanitary pads were delivered in Chattogram, and 100 handwashing devices were delivered in Bandarban. • BDRCS and the IFRC distributed 520 bottles of drinking water in Bandarban and Khagrachhari and deployed one water treatment unit in Bandarban. 2 Kancha houses are built primarily from temporary materials, including soil, wood, bamboo, straw and palm leaves, making them highly vulnerable to floods and landslides. Jhupri houses are even more fragile, typically featuring soil floors and walls, with roofs made from bamboo, straw, polythene or similar temporary materials.
Inter-Cluster Coordination Group Situation Report | 1 
 Inter-Cluster Coordination Group - Bangladesh 
• At least eight partners - BDRCS, BRAC, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, Oxfam, Save the Children, UNICEF-supported partners, World Vision and YPSA - are supporting operations, reaching approximately 15,000 households. Gaps & Constraints: • More than 20 unions remain inundated, with boat-only access in many remote and landslide-affected areas; damaged roads also restrict the deployment of mobile water treatment plants. • Inaccessibility, unsafe terrain and shortages of technical staff, particularly in the Chattogram Hill Tracts, are delaying assessments, field coordination and needs verification. • Power and telecommunications disruptions continue to affect reporting and coordination. Cross-cutting Areas Accountability to Affected Populations The Accountability to Affected People Working Group strengthened national coordination by sharing standardised messages on landslides, floods and snakebite prevention to support consistent and timely risk communication and community engagement. At the district level, District Information Offices in Bandarban, Khagrachhari and Rangamati, in coordination with the respective district administrations, are conducting community outreach through public announcements and other communication channels to promote evacuation, preparedness and risk-reduction measures. Imams affiliated with the Islamic Foundation are reinforcing these messages through mosques and community discussions, encouraging protective actions and broader community awareness. Gender in Humanitarian Action The Gender in Humanitarian Action (GiHA) Working Group (WG) and its local chapters supported the integration of gender, protection, inclusion and accountability considerations across the response. Aid Comilla mobilised 30 volunteers—25 women and five men—to conduct door-to-door information dissemination in Cox’s Bazar. PROTTYASHI, co-lead of the Chattogram local GiHA chapter, coordinated with local authorities, Disaster Management Committees, humanitarian partners and shelter management committees, and conducted gender-responsive shelter monitoring to identify safety, privacy, accessibility and protection concerns affecting women, girls, persons with disabilities and other at-risk groups. PROTTYASHI also disseminated early warning and preparedness information, shared emergency contact information, and provided two handheld microphones and 10 umbrellas to support public announcements, evacuation, and rescue coordination. RWDO, co-lead of the Sylhet local GiHA chapter, maintained coordination with government and local disaster management authorities, continued monitoring the situation and remained ready to support the response if conditions deteriorated. UTSA supported community-level loudspeaker announcements. The GiHA WG calls for accessible early warning and safe evacuation measures that respond to the specific needs of Indigenous communities, older persons, persons with disabilities, women, especially pregnant and lactating mothers, girls and other at-risk groups. The Working Group urges all sectors to integrate gender-based violence risk mitigation, safe spaces and confidential referral pathways into their response activities, while prioritising gender-responsive shelter, water, sanitation and hygiene, dignity assistance, menstrual hygiene management, maternal health and psychosocial support. It also advocates adequate resourcing and engagement with women-led organisations and local GiHA chapters to strengthen preparedness, targeted outreach, community feedback, and response delivery. Risk communication and relocation support, targeted support for the most vulnerable women and female-headed households, prevention of gender-based violence, and psychosocial support remain
Inter-Cluster Coordination Group Situation Report | 1 
 Inter-Cluster Coordination Group - Bangladesh 
essential for women and girls at heightened risk across the country. A Gender Alert has been published on 12 July, highlighting the differentiated impacts of monsoon flooding, flash floods, and landslide risks on women, girls, and other groups facing heightened vulnerability, and identifying urgent actions for government, humanitarian, and development partners. 
For further information, please contact: Lorenna Dib Oliveira, Inter-Cluster Coordination Group Chair, lorenna.diboliveira@un.org

related.title: United Nations Charter
related.summary: CHAPTER II MEMBERSHIP Article 3 The original Members of the United Nations shall be the states which, having participated in the United Nations Conference on International Organization at San Francisco, or having previ- ously signed the Declaration by United Nations of January 1,1942, sign the present Charter and ratify it in accordance with Article 110.
bullets: CHAPTER II MEMBERSHIP Article 3 The original Members of the United Nations shall be the states which, having participated in the United Nations Conference on International Organization at San Francisco, or having previ- ously signed the Declaration by United Nations of January 1,1942, sign the present Charter and ratify it in accordance with Article 110.

Article 5 / A Member of the United Nations against which preventive or enforcement action has been taken by the Security Council may be suspended from the exercise of the rights and privileges of mem- bership by the General Assembly upon the recom- mendation of the Security Council.

Article 6 A Member of the United Nations which has persistently violated the Principles contained in the present Charter may be expelled from the Organization by the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council.

related.excerpt: KYIV, Ukraine — Russian recruits arriving on the front lines in Ukraine survive an estimated 20 to 30 minutes before they are killed or wounded, Central Intelligence Agency Director John Ratcliffe said Wednesday, marking the first time a senior American intelligence official has confirmed how deadly the war has become for Moscow. The assessment comes as Ukraine’s battlefield technology has stalled Russia’s advance along the front and drawn foreign partners ready to spend billions of dollars in deals with its defense industry. European and Ukrainian officials have said for months that Russian casualty rates have climbed to record levels, with Ukraine’s top general telling NATO allies in May that Russia loses at least 1,000 soldiers a day. “Our intelligence is consistent with some of the open-source reporting you may have seen in Ukraine,” Ratcliffe said at the Defense and Innovation Summit in Pennsylvania, according to Bloomberg. “The average life expectancy of a Russian recruit right now, arriving on the battlefield in Ukraine, is estimated to be between 20 and 30 minutes.” “That’s because AI-powered drones have gotten to be such specialized, low-cost killing machines,” he added.
